utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr Dubuisson, can we have the accused in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before we start, my colleagues and myself beg for apology. We had a bureau meeting this morning, the recently constituted bureau as you know, so we started at 9.00 but we could not finish the meeting until now. Our apologies. We are going to resume our work. Can the booth hear me, are you ready, otherwise I will have to repeat my apology. Can everybody hear me? Fine. If everybody can hear me, I shall without further ado give the floor to Mr Harmon, who is going to introduce the next witness; a protected witness, I suppose, judging by the device that has been set in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr President, good morning counsel. Yes, Mr President, the next witness we will present is a protected witness. She will be identified as Witness O. The protections that will be available will be facial distortion and a pseudonym. She will be a short witness, Mr President. She is a Muslim woman who will testify about post-October 1992 events in respect of the collection of weapons from Muslims who lived in the area of Santici. She will testify about her observations on 15th April, pre-attack observations, and she will testify about the attack on her home and the murder of her husband in front of her and three small children on 16th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, so four items which shall be part of the testimony of this witness. Registrar, so we have a public hearing but with a partially closed session. Please have the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr President and your Honours, I will be asking at the end of her testimony to go into a private session to ask her to identify some photographs, two photographs of her late husband. I have advised her of the situation in this Trial Chamber in respect of those photographs, and she has informed me that she is able to make those identifications to your Honours. I will also be asking her about some other events that could indirectly identify her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Madam, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, we are going to call you Witness O. All you have to do is read your name as written on the paper handed in by the Registrar, just to make sure that it tallies with your identity, but you do not spell out your name. Thank you. You remain seated and you can read the declaration that is given to you. Witness O (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness O. You agreed to come to the Tribunal on the request made by the Prosecutor on the counts against the accused, General Blaskic. Your testimony, in principle, from what we are told, is going to deal with what you notice in October 1992 with the gathering of weapons that you could see, your observations before April 1993, the murder of your husband and more generally speaking, what you can say as to the attack in April 1993. You are going to be asked short questions as to your identity, but there is no danger attached to this because you are a protected witness, and then very freely, in your own words, you will make a statement in relation to the four points stated by the Prosecutor, briefly but as suits you. Then you will be asked questions by the Prosecutor and then by the Defence and finally by the judges. Mr Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr President. Good morning, Witness O.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Witness O, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: On 16th April 1993, did you live in Santici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Did you live in a house with your husband and your three small children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: What were the ages of your children in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My daughter was 10, my son was 8 and my other son was 7.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Now I would like to focus your attention on the gathering of guns in the possession of Muslims that occurred in October 1993. Can you tell the judges what you know about the collection of guns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In October 1992, a conflict broke out between the Croats and the Muslims. After it stopped, the conflict was a very short one, my husband was in charge of collecting weapons from Muslims who were in our immediate neighbourhood. He was supposed to collect these weapons and to hand them over to Nenad Santic. He gave him a little piece of paper saying that he would be allowed to move around and take weapons from these people who had weapons and that these weapons should be brought to him.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Did Nenad Santic make any threats in respect of Muslims who did not turn in their weapons? Can you describe that threat to the judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he threatened that if somebody would not turn his weapons in, his house could be burned down, and that he would not be safe in this area any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: On whose behalf was that threat issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On behalf of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Did your husband in fact collect weapons and turn them over to Nenad Santic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: How many weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were about six or seven rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Did those rifles include a rifle that he had himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Who was Nenad Santic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nenad Santic was the commander of the HVO in that area where we lived.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know who his commander was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to 16th April 1993. On the morning of 16th April 1993, did you have any weapons in your house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Prosecutor, I think this has been said already, I would rather the witness made her testimony, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr President, she is going to have to add one part to her testimony and the next question was going to permit her to make the narration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Okay, let us move ahead, because you specified the items that were relevant to this testimony and you may add on things if need be, but raise your question and then the witness can speak to the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will be very direct, Mr President. Witness O, did you have a pistol in your house on 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had a small pistol which my husband bought from his brother and he also had a licence allowing him to have this pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness O, would you please tell the judges what happened to you and to members of your family on 16th April 1993; in your own words, at your own pace.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the morning of April 16th, I was awakened by a strong explosion, a loud explosion. I was sleeping with my daughter and my husband was sleeping with the other children in another room. We all got up when we heard the explosion. We were sleeping upstairs, and we went downstairs then. He wore a blue coat that he would usually wear to work. We gathered around the stove. We heard shooting from all around, we did not know what was going on. My husband called our next door neighbour, who lived right next door, and he asked him whether he knew what was going on. He did not know himself. He brought some cigarettes and we both smoked a cigarette. While we were waiting there, there was a fence between our land and our neighbour's land, and we heard somebody jumping over that fence. They came to our land and they threw a hand grenade into the room. They started shooting at the door and a burst of gunfire opened the door and we heard a voice saying that we should get out. I said that I should only put socks on my children and I was told that they would not need them. My husband had that small pistol on his person, he took it to the staircase and threw it underneath the staircase. He went out first, he went to the door first, the door was open. He went out with his hands up. The person who opened our door was a person I did not see. As my husband was getting out, he was not facing this person, he had his back turned to this person who was commanding us, telling us what to do. As soon as he walked out, he started shooting at my husband all over him, from head to toes, and he fell. I took the children and I walked back in and I sat down and waited. Another soldier, who was on the other side, broke our glass door and said that we should get out. Not much time went by, perhaps a minute or two, he walked in with my mother-in-law, he walked into our house and he said that we should get out. My children were crying. I took them with me and we went out. I, my children, my father-in-law and my mother-in-law. That is how we left the house.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Now let me ask you some questions. Witness O, do you know the approximate time that you heard the explosion that awakened everybody in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was early in the morning, perhaps between 5.30 and 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Was your husband executed in your presence and the presence of your three children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: You said that a soldier came into the house with your mother-in-law. Can you describe how that soldier was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Did he have his face uncovered or covered, or do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, his face was not covered.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe the insignia that you saw on that particular soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that he had a patch with black on the back and a chess board sign on it. The chess board was red and white.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: During that same timeframe, did you also see other soldiers near your mother-in-law's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in front of her door there were soldiers too. I saw them through the window.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately how many soldiers did you see by your mother-in-law's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about three or four soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: When you left your house, how were you dressed and how were your children dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all wearing our pyjamas. We had been asleep, so we went downstairs. We did not know what was ahead of us and we did not know whether we should get dressed and we did not know what would happen to us and whether things that happened to other people would happen to us too, and things like that which happened at our door.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Within a matter of minutes, within five minutes of leaving your house, did you look back in the direction of your house, and if so, can you tell the judges what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I turned around and the house was already on fire. When we left the house, I asked which direction we should go in, and we were told and we set out. Less than five minutes had gone by and our house was on fire. You could see that by the windows, as we looked at the windows we saw the fire. Perhaps the curtain started burning immediately. At any rate, you could see the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr President, now I would request that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Right. Registrar, can you see to it that it is done?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We are now in the open session and I will call you Witness O. Could you now please tell me, without mentioning any names, was your husband a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband was listed as a member of the Territorial Defence, but he did not perform any duties. He did not go to the frontline, he had work duty in the company where he worked. When this happened, he was on hold in his company.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Tell me, your husband's neighbours who were in the TO from Zume, did they go to the frontlines or were they mostly in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the neighbourhood, these were all men who had families. I think that nobody went.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Nobody went where, to fight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Just so that it is clear in the transcript. Tell me, did your husband have any guard duties, watches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the conflict which happened in late April, after that he surrendered his weapons and after that, they simply could come in front of their houses and keep watch. The Croats around our houses just simply told us that we need not be afraid, that should any problems arise that they would protect us.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: You probably got confused, you said, "after the conflict in April, he did not have any arms". You probably thought April 1992 -- you probably thought October 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: So did he go and perform guard duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, no, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Did your father-in-law go and perform any guard duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe out of fear that something would happen, he would often -- we were very afraid down there, we knew that we were in a difficult position.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: And your mother-in-law, we will not mention her name, says that he was the commander of the guard there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was listed as such, but he never arranged any guard duties which were being conducted, the way it was supposed to be -- he was listed as being in charge of the guards in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Did your father-in-law have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: When your husband surrendered those six rifles to Santic, did Santic request that all weapons be surrendered, that is pistols in addition to the rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He requested that every man surrender one rifle each; he did not say to turn over -- I do not know, I did not talk to him. He simply came and said that the weapons needed to be surrendered to him.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: You said that Santic made threats. In what words? Did you hear that from Santic or did your husband tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband decided immediately that he would turn over the rifle because we were there and the children were there. He feared that somebody might not turn over the rifles and there would be problems that someone -- houses may be torched.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Was he afraid that someone's houses may be burnt or did Santic tell him explicitly that they would be burnt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happened that some Muslim houses be torched overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: So based on the fact that some Muslim houses were burned overnight, your husband was afraid that it might happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: I will restate the question. Did Nenad Santic directly tell your husband that he will torch his house if he did not surrender the weapons, or did he fear that they might be torched if the Muslims did not surrender the arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that after the conflict in October happened, and many of our Muslim neighbours left their houses with their weapons, he said that if they wanted to return to their homes, and also those who did not leave their homes, he said that everybody should turn over their weapons to him, if they wanted to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: This is all that Santic told your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not there, this is what I was --

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: You mean your husband told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: And that was all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: I conclude from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The witness has already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well, thank you, we can move on. You said that Cerkez was Santic's superior, Mario Cerkez. How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Santic was the commander of the HVO in the area where I lived, and Mario Cerkez was the commander of the HVO for the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez was the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Not the commander for the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to know, when you started talking about the interesting events in April 1992, 15th April, you mentioned that these buyers came and I guess they bought some, what, concrete blocks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you think that that was interesting to mention in the context of your testimony? What did you think or what did you conclude that these blocks were for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably they were going to serve to make some shelters or some barricades, but it was interesting, it was curious, because for a long time, there were no buyers and on that day, all of a sudden the traffic was much greater and up until then there was almost none.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: So you concluded that this was supposed to be used for defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: So was it for defence or for attack? What are these concrete blocks used for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They could be used to also prepare the positions from which there would be an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: But they cannot be moved. Never mind. Did something happen on 15th April that the Croat population needed to buy these blocks to protect themselves? Did you see something, did you see something on television that something happened, for instance in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Zenica, Zivko Totic was arrested, he was arrested and as far as I can recall, there were negotiations between these two sides, and the two sides could not come to an agreement. When I came home, my late husband said that he watched television and he was nervous, he was afraid, he said that he heard on television that Kordic was saying that there are no more negotiations with the Muslims, and he said that if there are no more negotiations, the only option is war. He was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Was this an arrest or was this a kidnapping and killing of four people? Did any kind of authority arrest Zivko Totic, or was he kidnapped, abducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said what I had to say because I was not ...

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Very well. On the checkpoint where you saw the soldiers, did you notice their insignia? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went through the checkpoint without looking at the soldiers because I was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Do you recall what kind of uniforms they wore, black or camouflage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: On this critical day, did you call Mirjan Kupreskic, did you talk to him on the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: What was it about, if you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was not me who called him, I think it was my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: You do not know the contents of their conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much, Mr President, we have concluded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr Prosecutor, did you want to add anything to your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Witness O, let me clarify a point in your testimony. Did your late husband tell you that Nenad Santic told him that if the Muslims did not turn in their guns that Muslim homes would be torched?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr President, this was discussed both in the examination-in-chief and in the cross-examination. This is repetitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you say what is not a repetition in your question? If it is only to repeat a previous question, a prior question, it is not necessary, I agree with Mr Nobilo there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr President, I understand. The witness has given an answer on direct examination that differs from her answer on cross-examination and for purposes of clarification with that one question I think I can resolve the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then we would propose a non-leading question, your Honour, not that a leading question be used to try and clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Put a question that does not have the answer in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am happy to do so, Mr President. Witness O, what exactly did your husband tell you Nenad Santic had told him would happen about the guns and the failure of Muslims to turn in guns?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Look at the judges, if you do not mind, because you are speaking to the Tribunal, to the court. Do relax. Just answer the way that pleases you, that is all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband said that if the Muslims, that October when the conflict took place, if the Muslims did not turn in their weapons, that they could not survive there and that their houses would be burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did your husband say that he had been informed of that by Nenad Santic, or did he come to that conclusion on his own, independent of anything Nenad Santic had told him?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Leading, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: True, I think we can stay on that, I think we are sufficiently informed on this matter. Equally, even if belatedly, I remind Mr Nobilo of this: the question related to the phone call to Kupreskic had not been mentioned in the examination-in-chief, unless I am wrong. Do you have another question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Mr President, I have concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, I am now turning to my colleagues, to my fellow judges, before you finish your testimony. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to have some information about what happened in October 1992. You said there was a short conflict. You were there at that time in Santici. What was this conflict, can you just describe it? What happened exactly in that conflict, and when did it stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conflict took place in the latter part of October, it lasted only one day. In fact it was not a real conflict that took place there, the real conflict took place somewhere else. The HVO soldiers went and I think that the real conflict took place in Novi Travnik. The villagers from Ahmici, the Muslims set up a barricade so that the soldiers, the Croats, could not pass through; so that the road would simply be cut off for them. I think that as I recall, that was the reason, so it was not a real conflict which took place, so the conflict was provoked from somewhere else, the conflict took place somewhere else and the HVO soldiers started towards the area where this conflict took place and the locals from Ahmici, the Muslims, set up a barricade so that they could not pass through, so that the conflict would not become even greater.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: In other words, in October and after October until April 1993, there was no Muslim attack in Santici? The Muslims did not attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: There was no attack. When you said that Nenad Santic told your husband that the punishment for having any weapon would be to have the house burnt and to be -- not to be able to survive in Santici, this Nenad Santic, was he a military commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: What was his role? He was a military commander. And his threat was being fulfilled on a large scale to many houses, or just to few people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Partially in small proportions, people who were in our immediate neighbourhood who were living along the road, I think that it was only they who turned in their weapons so that they would be safe in their homes and that they would not fear.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Were they safe in their homes? Those who turned in weapons, did they stay safely in their homes, or did they have to leave -- all Muslims had to leave Santici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: After these events of April 15th, 16th, did all Muslims leave Santici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: All of them? Did they come back after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we all left.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: So there are no Muslims left in Santici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were told to go, that we could not live there any more.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: How many Muslims were there in Santici? Was it a majority of Muslims or a majority of Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: So the minority of Muslims was completely -- had to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: You told the court that your husband told you of a statement made by Mr Kordic. Did you yourself know Mr Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only through television. I watched him.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: How often did you see him on television? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall the number of times, but I did see him a number of times on television.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: When you saw him on television, was anyone with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Tell me about these cinder blocks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Are you feeling better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Good. These cinder blocks were manufactured by the factory in which you were working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: What were they intended to be used for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was meant for construction, for construction of different structures. But it could have been used for different purposes, not only the buildings but also fences.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: These blocks were bought by a number of people. Could you tell us whether those people were Muslims or Croats or both Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These people were dressed in camouflage clothes. At that time, Muslims could not move about in the camouflage uniform in Vitez; in other words he may have but he would have run the risk of maybe being beaten up or even arrested. It was simply better for them not to move about so in these camouflage clothes, so I could say that these were Croats, because I cannot say that I saw a Muslim who was moving around in the camouflage clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is nearly over. I wanted to put a last question to you. Before you came to the Tribunal, and also at the time of those tragic events, had you heard of the General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR HARMON
utterances.text: Could you specify -- did you see him, did you see him on television, did you have the feeling that he was playing a major part? Could you say this to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw him on television. What duty he was on, that I cannot explain and I do not know. I only remember seeing him on television and that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. It is over, it was not too long, you are going to recover, have a rest and return to where you live in the hope that you can forget all these tragic events. Please do not move from your seat, the judges are going to withdraw for a break, and we are going to resume at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please bring in the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Kehoe, I know that you are the one who is going to take the examination-in-chief of the next witness. Could you tell us the identity of that witness and what you expect from that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr President, good morning. Thank you, good morning, your Honours. The next witness is company Sergeant Major Stephen Hughes of the Cheshire Regiment, first battalion. Along with the other British contingent, British soldiers that the court has heard, they are all part of the Cheshire Regiment stationed in the Bila camp right outside of Vitez from October 1992 through approximately 11th May 1993. He will testify concerning 16th April, where he and his platoon of Warriors went through the outside part of Stari Vitez and saw Croat soldiers with ribbons on their shoulders, identifying ribbons as the court has heard on other occasions, going house to house in a systematic fashion, giving the appearance of rooting those people out. He will also testify about the shooting of at least two civilians, bodies he saw on the ground and he likewise will talk on the 16th about artillery fire coming into the location where he was in Stari Vitez; he will likewise note that there was no return fire, nor did he see any Bosnian soldiers on the 16th. We move to the 17th, Mr President, your Honours. The witness will testify concerning a movement of refugees south of -- moving from the direction of Santici towards the Dubravica school, a long column of refugees that he believed to be Muslim civilians. As we move further up that road, as your Honours know, the location of the bungalow is located. He will testify concerning parking near that bungalow on the 17th and observing an anti-aircraft weapon up on the bluff above the bungalow on the other side of the street firing into the area, and he does not know the exact location, but firing into the area anywhere from Pirici, Ahmici et cetera, those villages on the other side of the road. He will likewise testify during this timeframe of on an evening seeing a village in Putis Loncari area, a Muslim village, moving into those villages and seeing much of that village burnt, evidence that the villagers had left in haste and also evidence that the houses themselves had been looted. He will testify down the line of having returned to that village and all the looted items, such as it was, et cetera, were gone. He will likewise testify concerning several events briefly concerning the truck bomb on 18th April 1993. He was present, one of the first Warriors there, took his photographs, assisted in the evacuation of civilians and assisted the next day in the evacuation of the dead. As your Honours know, on 21st April there was a cease-fire conference attended by General Petkovic, General Halilovic as well as ECMM representatives and BritBat representatives. As you will recall from Major Watters' testimony, one of the jobs of the British battalion was to ensure that the armies moved back from the confrontation line and thereafter to have the respective generals to convince their soldiers to move back from those lines. Sergeant Major Hughes and his company, or his platoon, did exactly that, and they took General Petkovic around, as well as General Halilovic, and one of the places they took General Petkovic as part of this was to the bungalow, where they had a discussion in the bungalow. His last item of evidence, Mr President, is the burial in Stari Vitez, he participated in a body exchange with the HVO where he gave them three bodies of Croats and in return got 96 Muslims for burial and there will be a short video on that, Mr President and your Honours. That is the summary of Sergeant Major Hughes' testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Congratulations on behalf of my fellow colleagues. Are you sure you want to have the witness after all this? Congratulations anyway. As we are now accustomed, you let the witness speak in his or her own words and you only intervene on the points that are relevant to you, because we were able, as you have just shown, to show the essential items. Let us have Sergeant Major Hughes in. How much time did you devote to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe, Mr President, we could be done in two, two and a half hours, somewhere in that location. The reason I hesitate on the actual time, Mr President, is there will be some drawing on the maps and locations and sometimes that takes a little bit more time than I anticipate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay. Let us have the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr President, I believe the usher just went to get the witness from the witness room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In the meantime, may I just know, he is a sergeant major? I have not been in the British army. What is a sergeant major?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They move up ranks naturally, Judge. One of the upper ranks, the warrant officer ranks are sergeant major and regimental sergeant major, a sergeant major being a warrant officer second class and a regimental sergeant major being the highest ranking enlisted soldier, who is a warrant officer first class. As you move down from there, you move to the regular non-commissioned levels, from staff sergeant to sergeant, corporal, lance corporal, private soldier. I may be missing a rank or two in there, Judge Riad. Naturally Sergeant Major Hughes can answer that better than I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Sergeant Major? Can you state your name, your first name and your rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear you. My first name is Stephen Hughes, my rank is WO2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are going to read the declaration handed to you by the usher. This is your oath. SERGEANT MAJOR HUGHES (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, please sit down, Sergeant Major. Your grade and your hierarchy let you come in as a witness in this trial against General Blaskic, who is present in the courtroom. Whilst you were stationed in the area involved in the events, you took part in the events of 16th April, you attended and you were witness to a number of events, artillery fire and movements of refugees. You noted many things such as villages on fire and you have things to tell us about the truck bomb and also you will talk to the conference or negotiations on the cease-fire. You will be guided by the Prosecutor. Once a few questions have been put to you as a preliminary matter, you can be free to state in your own words what you have to say. If there are missing elements, Mr Kehoe will, on behalf of the Prosecution, see to it that he puts the questions that are relevant to the trial. You are used to being very synthetical, that is what you learn in the army, so you have the floor, Mr Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr President. Good afternoon. Could you give us your rank in the British army, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is warrant officer class 2.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: What is your title in the British army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sergeant Major.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Sergeant Major Hughes, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 39.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: How long have you been in the British army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been in just over 22 and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say you have been in the British army your entire adult life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: What regiment do you belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I belong to the Cheshire Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Have you been in the Cheshire Regiment the past 22 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, Sergeant Major, that you are a professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the period of time where the Cheshire Regiment was assigned as peace keeping efforts in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Were you part of those efforts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly was.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: During what period of time were you in Bosnia-Herzegovina with the Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From late November to, I recall, May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr President, before the witness gives his actual events of what took place there, I just want to ask the witness what his actual job in the theatre was. If you could, Sergeant Major Hughes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My job was platoon commander of II Platoon, A Company.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: In a little bit more detail, Sergeant Major, can you explain to the court what that means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That means I was in command of a platoon, which is approximately 26 men. The platoon consisted of three sections, commanded by a corporal in each, and I commanded four Warrior fighting vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: So you were part of A Company and in A Company there were three platoons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You were the commander of the second platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: In your platoon, how many Warriors did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: In your own words, Sergeant Major, let me direct your attention to the outbreak of hostilities in the Lasva Valley in and around 16th April 1993. Can you tell the court your observations during that period of time, up through the burial of the 96 bodies in Stari Vitez on 28th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On 16th April, we received information that there was disturbances in the town of Vitez. We were tasked to go into Vitez and obviously look at the situation and see what information we could gather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please slow down a little. Remember the interpreters. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we approached Vitez, moved into the Muslim area, the old town of Vitez. At that stage, there were a number of civilians to one side of the road, as we approached the centre of Vitez, who were coming under fire. At that stage, I placed my vehicle between them and the fire, to protect a woman that was crawling along the pavement, so she could get into cover. Once that was complete, I continued into Vitez, to the junction by the hotel in the centre of Vitez. From there, we could observe what I saw as HVO soldiers moving through towards the old part of Vitez. We continued to move around the area, noting that at that stage what looked to be, as I say, an attack on to the Muslim area of Vitez. The following day, the 17th, I was tasked out to the area east of Vitez, to the town or village of Jelinak Putis. Also during that time, I was in the area of the bungalow and it was at this stage, observing the area to the south, that I spotted what I believed to be some form of anti-tank weapon or anti-aircraft weapon. Again at that stage, I took some time to identify, using binoculars and then finally the gunsight, which had a better magnification, which more or less confirmed to me that there was something there. Eventually the weapon was fired, and that gave me then a definite identification that it was some form of anti-aircraft weapon. Then the following day, the 18th, I was tasked again to go into Vitez. On this occasion we were blocked from entering by a large petrol tanker across the road. We decided to turn round, move around and try and approach Vitez from the east; again, there was no access, or access was denied by a tractor across the bridge and some anti-tank mines laid on the floor. We then moved back round again and made a second attempt to enter Vitez. On this occasion, they had moved the petrol tanker more towards the west, and this gave us the opportunity to outflank the checkpoint and enter into Vitez itself. Having negotiated past the checkpoint at this stage I was engaged by about five or six occupants of the checkpoint, hitting the rear of the vehicle. However, I continued on the task that day. On returning back from that task, on the way out, the petrol tanker had been moved and was no longer in sight, and the road was free to move back out. During this time, I was at the garage which was our echelon and the large explosion was heard from the vicinity of Vitez. We were later then tasked to enter Vitez to discover what the situation was, and on approaching into the old town of Vitez, due to the fact that I was first in, there was a lot of devastation. The point of the blast had caused a small crater in the road and all that was remaining of the vehicle was the rear chassis, a number of vehicles. At that stage, we moved around to try and get a full assessment of the situation. Then from there, it was decided that it would be safe to move out the people from that area, and evacuate them to Travnik. The following day, the 19th, again we were tasked to go back in and remove any dead bodies from the scene of the explosion, and also to remove what body parts were found to be in the area of the centre of the blast. Then over the next few days we were tasked to local areas, especially on the 22nd, to go north of Vitez and monitor the areas, to see how the cease-fire was holding up, and whether there was any change in the situation regarding the position of BiH and HVO soldiers. Then on the 28th, I was tasked to pick up General Petkovic and General Halilovic, and with an interpreter and a member of the ECMM, to go round north of Vitez and take both parties to the various positions in that area; again to look to see if they were withdrawing back to their original positions before the fighting within the Vitez area began. It was during this stage that we went to the bungalow and as a point, whilst in there, an individual HVO soldier got quite irate and from the information I got from the interpreter, he was indicating that he, or his family had been killed, and that UNPROFOR had stood by and watched. He was swinging a pistol around. Eventually went outside, he tried to get to the vehicle holding the BiH commanders. However, he was unsuccessful in that and eventually he was calmed down and taken away. We continued on with the varying tasks with both parties, eventually finishing off in Vitez itself, visiting the BiH headquarters and various positions around the village. Then on the 29th, I was tasked to go into Vitez to do a body exchange. This consisted of going into the old part of Vitez, the Muslim area, where we picked up approximately three bodies, transported them to the school in Vitez where they were taken into the school and then in exchange, we picked up approximately 94 to 96 Muslim bodies, and these were transported to a burial area in, again, the old town, the Muslim part of Vitez, where they were eventually buried there in a mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr President, with your permission, Sergeant Major, I would just like to ask you several questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ask several questions about the events that you just discussed. On the morning of 16th April, you said that you went into old Vitez. Approximately what time was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Difficult to assess the time of the morning. It was about mid morning, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you tell the court what path you took coming into old Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came on the main road into Vitez from the west, passing the garage which was our echelon, which then brought us in to the old town or the old part of Vitez, which was the direct route in, which would take you then right into the centre of Vitez itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr President, with your permission, if I could have Sergeant Major Hughes step up to what has been put on the easel. For the record, Mr President, that is 45F. If I may approach?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sergeant Major, using the yellow marker, can you just designate the road that you used coming into Stari Vitez on the morning of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You are marking that in yellow. During your narrative to the judges, you also said that you saw a series of HVO soldiers that were going from house to house. Before we mark that, did these soldiers have anything identifying themselves to each other on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had ribbons tied to the shoulders of their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: As a professional soldier, what did you understand those ribbons to mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To me, it gave an indication of what particular unit they came from, what area. It is so that they between themselves could identify themselves, because in that situation both, I would say, opposing forces wore the same uniforms, so without the markings, it would be difficult to identify who was HVO and who may have been BiH soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: So in simple terms, they would put that coloured ribbon on so they did not shoot each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You stated that you saw them moving, these soldiers with the ribbons, moving in a particular area on the map. Could you take the pink and square out or circle out the area where you saw them moving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you make that a little darker so they can see it on the camera? Sergeant Major, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time they were moving through this part, they were moving towards the west, again towards the old part of Vitez. They were moving in what I would call a house clearing method, they were fire, manoeuvre and sort of covering each other, which to me looked, as I say, similar sorts of drills that we would use when moving through a built-up area.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you and the British army call this fighting in built-up areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Sergeant, when you saw them moving from house to house, did you see anybody firing at them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see any Muslim, Bosnian Muslim soldiers around that period of time moving in that area to oppose them or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you move to another location thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I moved round and came through round to this road and then eventually I waited in this area here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were in that particular area, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was what I believed to be either an artillery or mortar round landed approximately 50 metres to my front in this position here.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you mark that in red with an M?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you put a circle around it so we can see it? You said that this was either an artillery round or a mortar round?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you tell the difference at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not really at that particular time. But again, on reflection, the amount of explosion and dust, smoke that came up maybe it was a smaller round than artillery so it could more likely be a mortar round.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: This was an incoming round?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see any rounds going back out in response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, none at all.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Earlier in your testimony, you mentioned that you saw a woman that was crawling along the pavement, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did she appear to be a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Was she wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that particular time I did not notice if she was wounded, she was just crawling along the pavement.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you notice later on if she was wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we came back round again, we pulled up to where the woman had moved into a protected area, into a little alley way, and there was a number of people gesturing to us to help, because she had been shot. Looking down again, a limited view because we were closed down and therefore I was looking through the observation post scopes, is that she was lying on the floor and I later learnt from another vehicle -- we moved off, another vehicle then came in and treated the woman for a gunshot wound to the chest.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you take a green marker and mark the location of that wound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You can have a seat, Sergeant Major. You have marked that exhibit in the lower left-hand corner of the area that you said the soldiers were going from house to house, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we move ahead to the events that take place after this, when you saw this going on, Sergeant Major, as a professional soldier, did you come to any conclusions as to what was happening in that area with those HVO soldiers going from house to house and moving in towards Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the conclusion I came to was that it was the normal practice, I would say, for anyone that wishes to clear an area, and obviously take control of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You had occasion, the next day, to continue to patrol around Stari Vitez, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr President, we have a series of photographs that are marked as Exhibit 152, they are a series of photographs that detail several issues in Sergeant Major Hughes' testimony. Right now we would like to deal with the first two, 152/1 and 152/2, and with the assistance of the usher, if we could put those on the ELMO. Sergeant Major Hughes, we are looking at Exhibit 152/1. Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: What is that of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a photograph looking west towards the quarry on the outskirts of Vitez and obviously to the left-hand side near the car is the body of a young boy.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next photograph, Mr Usher, 152/2. What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the same body from the previous photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see him in or about this time lying on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Approximately how old was this young boy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By, obviously, body size, I would say that -- you know, a young teenager, no older than maybe 17 or below that.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Was it clear to you at that juncture that he was dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Usher, we can turn off the ELMO. If we can leave those photographs there because we will be having the usher return to discuss the other photographs. Sergeant Major Hughes, you said that on the 17th that you went up to the bungalow area, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I am sorry to get you up again, but if we could flip over Exhibit 45F. Underneath that, Mr President, should be Exhibit 56F. Again if I can ask Sergeant Major Hughes to step up to the microphone and if I can approach the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just a specification, what is the number of this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am sorry, this map is 53C.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sergeant Major Hughes, you stated that you went up to the area of the bungalow -- did you call it the bungalow, by the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we called it the Swiss cottage.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that designated on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You said that you saw -- can you take the yellow marker and just mark the area where you were located when you went up there on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You likewise said that you saw an anti-aircraft weapon. Can you take the red marker -- actually if you can do it with this marker, and mark with a circle the general area where you saw that artillery piece.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you make it thick so it can show up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: To get closer to the map, Mr Hayman, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sergeant Major, you were looking at that location with a set of binoculars, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: And also your gunsight in the Warrior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were in that location, did you see someone that you thought was a forward observer, or a spotter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you explain to the judges what a forward observer or a spotter is? You can turn this way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What it is is that a forward observer or spotter is somebody who will move forward of what we would call a gun line, i.e. mortars or artillery, who is in view of the area that he wishes the rounds from that particular gun line, whether again it is mortars or artillery, land, so therefore he can be in touch with the gun line and tell them any corrections that they need to make; in other words, are the rounds dropping short of the target, too far off the target or are they actually on target.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, Sergeant Major Hughes, that any army that has artillery normally employs a spotter or forward observer to assist them as to where to direct the fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: The British army does as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You knew when you saw this guy up there what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: The basic range of fire from that location, what would have been the range of fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, depending on the piece of equipment that they were using, from that area if they were using an anti-aircraft weapon or of similar description, then you may be looking at maximum effective as two kilometres, 2,000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: So two kilometres out. How about the breadth of fire from left to right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the high ground, from the position they were in, they would reach no further south than along the edge of the valley, but from there again they would have a good arc coming through, down, because again this high ground here, coming down towards the Ahmici area and beyond (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say from their location they would have a -- excuse me -- direction of fire covering Ahmici, Pirici and all the way down into the Santici area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: It is a little awkward here, excuse me. When you were up there, did anybody leave that location and come down and see you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, while we were observing the position a small vehicle left, came down the winding road, down. Eventually, as it got closer, we identified it as a Suzuki-type Jeep that pulled up the other side of the bridge in front of us and the individuals got out and sort of indicated to us that they wanted us to turn our gun position, or our gun away from observing their position on top of the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you watch the track that they were using as they came down to your location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We watched it. A couple of times it went out of sight, due to trees, hedgerows et cetera, but we basically monitored it coming down -- we wanted to see where it was coming, because we were not aware it was going to come down to our position.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you take the track and with that red pen could you mark the approximate track that they came down to meet you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: So based on that, the sketch you just gave with the red markings down that track, they came out in the approximate location where you were on the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: After they spoke to you and asked you to retrain your gun, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see where they went after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they drove from there then and they went to the bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you take that back down the road and then circle the area where they went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on that, did you conclude that the soldiers and their firing were connected with the soldier at the bungalow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Prior to that time, had you seen soldiers in and about that bungalow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had seen soldiers on many occasions around the bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Virtually every time you drove past there were soldiers outside that bungalow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can stay on the 17th, on another occasion on that road did you observe a column of Muslims moving down towards the mountain road going from Dubravica to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you use a green pen, if you will, here is one right here, and mark the approximate area where they were and the direction with an arrow, the direction that they were going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You marked that in green, did you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Sergeant Major, approximately how many people did you see in that column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say between 50, 60.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: When you saw them, did you reach any conclusions as to whether or not they were Croat or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I reached the conclusion they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Why did you reach that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mainly the way the women were dressed, in the normal pantaloon-type Muslim clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: What was the makeup of these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Young and old, old men, old women, children. They were not complete as a group, they were stretched out along that particular part of the road and all heading west.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Walking in the direction of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were on the north side of the road, i.e. this side of the road (indicates), walking west towards the junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr President, if I could ask Sergeant Major Hughes to take a seat again, we will move along. Sergeant Major, before we move away from this particular exhibit, the soldiers that came down from the artillery point that you saw moving, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were dressed in camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said that you had gone past this particular -- you call it Swiss cottage, it is marked as the bungalow, several times. If we can move to the next photograph, which is 152/3. Mr President, your Honours and Defence counsel, there is a black and white copy here, we will substitute it with a colour copy when we have it available, which should be some time this afternoon. For the record, Mr President, this photograph, the individual in this photograph is not a member of the Cheshire Regiment, this individual's name was then Captain Lee Whitworth, who was part of the Prince of Wales' own Regiment of Yorkshire. They replaced the Cheshires in October 1993. We are introducing this evidence simply for the structure itself and not the individual that is in there. However, it is the only photograph in our possession of the structure before it was destroyed. Sergeant Major, turning to this particular exhibit, 152/3, is that the structure that you called the Swiss cottage or the bungalow, as it is designated on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr Usher. We are now going to move on. We will get to those photographs in one second. Sergeant Major, during this period of time, did you go to various locations over the course of your day, other than the locations that you have just testified about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise on the 17th, did you go to an area that you knew to be, as Sivrino Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you observe on 17th April in the area of Sivrino Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I observed a building or house which to me was not a completed building, in other words there were no windows in, et cetera. There was a number of refugees, what I would class as refugees in the houses, and at that particular time, there was incoming artillery or mortar fire into that general area, not necessarily directed at the house but into the general area or vicinity of where that building was. The people in there, from what I could observe obviously, were extremely concerned and worried, frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: I am just waiting for the translation. Sergeant Major, did you reach any conclusions as to whether or not these frightened people were Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, due to the way they were dressed was again yes, that they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Sergeant Major, prior to the events on 16th April, did the Cheshire Regiment on occasion send Warriors to the coal mines in Breza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The idea behind was that the coal mine at Vares or Breza was close to the Serb lines and on occasion was coming under direct mortar and artillery fire. It was felt that to keep or try and get parts of the infrastructure going within the area is -- the need for coal was important to take to the power stations, obviously to eventually generate electricity that was needed et cetera, so it was agreed upon that on a daily basis that two Warriors would be deployed there through the daylight hours, basically, hopefully, as a deterrent for the Bosnian Serbs engaged in the coal yard itself.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Sergeant Major, I apologise but I have been informed that you and I are moving quickly. After I finish asking a question, if you just pause a bit and give the interpreters a chance, I think it will be a bit better for the understanding of all involved. This covering of the coal mines in Breza, did you essentially abandon that when the hostilities broke out on 16th April, or certainly during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: When you returned back to your camp from Breza, did you take what you know as the bypass road, the Zenica bypass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: In the evening prior to this time, coming back from Breza, did you observe anything one evening on your way back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the way back I observed to the north, which indicated to me on the map that it was the villages of Putis and Jelinak, that you could see the glow of what I would get the impression of as buildings on fire. You could not actually see the buildings but you could see the glow in the dark from just behind the high ground.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: If the events in Ahmici that you testified previously to took place on 16th April, when approximately did you drive by and see the glow in the dark in Putis and Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say approximately around the same period.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, if I could then move to the next map. For the record, the map that we have is a copy of Exhibit 59 and marked 59B, if I am not mistaken, Mr Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Mr President, if I could ask Sergeant Major Hughes to step up to the map with a red pen. Now Sergeant Major, if I may, before we begin that, could you take the yellow pen and just mark what you know as the Zenica bypass that you would take going back to camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You said in and about this time you turned off the Zenica bypass and went into the village around Putis and Jelinak. Is the track that you took depicted on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Using the red pen, could you just draw that track?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You have designated on the map in red the track that you took on that first time you went in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You can have a seat, Sergeant Major. Sergeant Major, the first night that you saw that area aglow, did you go into the village that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not that night, no.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Approximately how many days after the first time you saw it did you go into that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately two days.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges what you observed when you went into that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we approached the village from the main Zenica/Vitez bypass, we moved up along the track. As we moved up the track towards the main part of the village, we noticed on either side of the road that there were piles of televisions and other valuables from the various houses placed out on the side of the track. We progressed up until we came to the main village of Jelinak. At that stage, I decided to dismount from the vehicle. Myself and one other then did a cursory search or walk round of the village, due to the fact that at this stage we had been warned that any cleared villages may have booby-traps or trip wires, so we proceeded with caution. Entered a number of houses, which gave me the indication that the houses themselves had been rapidly vacated. In some houses there was still food on the tables, the houses still had their clothes, valuables and goods in there. We noticed on numerous doors bullet holes around the door handle, again which indicated to us that they had fired at the door handles to get into locked buildings. There were a number of houses that had been burnt down, obviously the previous -- a number of days before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Kehoe, if you have finished your questions in a sequence that makes sense, we could have a break and resume at 3.00. Did you want to specify anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr President. Actually I was waiting previously for the translation, but if I could just finish this particular series, it is just two more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sergeant Major, you had during your period of time seen the burnt-out houses in Ahmici, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: The houses in this area, Putis and Jelinak, were they similar to those houses in their burnt-out condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, similar.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You said that you walked around after you and another soldier got out of the Warriors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: When walking around, did you draw any conclusions as to what ethnic group owned the houses that were burnt out and vacated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority indicated to me that they were Muslim in the way of their design, and the depiction -- a lot of the houses have the Muslim crescent on the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on that Muslim crescent, you believe that the house belonged to a Bosnian Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr President, I believe this is an appropriate time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned. We will resume our work at 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Mr Registrar, would you have General Blaskic come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, is it possible to have the witness in?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As I said at the outset of the testimony of Sergeant Major Hughes, several photographs that are in the court's package and that were likewise in the Defence package were in black and white.
