utterances.text: It was difficult to assess at that stage. At that particular point, Colonel Stewart, the commanding officer, arrived on the scene and again he pointed out -- there was a television crew with them and he pointed out to the television crew that the majority of houses were Muslim. I would say that some of the houses that were burnt were a mix of some Croat and some Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: A more general question. Judging by your long stay, which is from November until May, November 1992 until May 1993, and your knowledge of the parties there, do you consider the HVO as an orderly and disciplined army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I seen, they were, of the two, obviously yes, were the better equipped and in a lot of cases seemed to be more in control than the BiH counterparts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Sergeant Major, you spent some time on the ground in this area, and you were a military man. I take it in the course of your activities and observations there you became familiar with all the military organisations in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We became familiar with who was in the area and who was defending what area. What individual units and who they belonged to and who they were commanded by we were not overfamiliar with, but we knew what areas were HVO-, what areas were BiH-controlled, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You are speaking of two principal military structures, the BiH Army, I take it that was on one side, and the other side the HVO, is that what you are speaking to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: In answer to my brother Riad, you said the HVO was a disciplined force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that there was -- more in the Vitez area anyway, there seemed to be more command and control with the HVO soldiers which, as I say, in the Vitez area we had more dealings with, as the BiH forces were more out of the area of Vitez itself.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Do I take it that on the Croatian side it is your judgment that the HVO was in a position to exercise military control over the areas you have described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you become aware of the person who was in charge of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the only time was the date already mentioned when I picked up initially General Petkovic. That gave me an indication, at that stage, of who the commander was.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: All these places you have referred to were in Central Bosnia, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the HVO have a command structure relating to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the whole of Central Bosnia, I maybe could not answer that question, but for the area that we operated in, then, as I am aware, they had the command structure within our area of responsibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Although you did not become aware of his identity, you would know that the HVO structure fell under the command of a single person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were aware. At that stage, unfortunately, we did not take much notice of names of people who were in command, because there were other jobs and other tasks to get on with, so we knew that they had a command structure, but again, we were not aware of who was commanding who and who was commanding what districts, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me ask you one last question. Were there things which happened as described by you capable of happening beyond the knowledge of the HVO authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would say not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Sergeant Major, you have just about finished. Only a couple of pieces of information in order to better know and understand what happened. You said that you were shot at, people shot at your Warrior vehicle. What were the instructions of UNPROFOR if there was direct firing and aggressive firing at UNPROFOR forces? What did your superiors say and what were the general instructions about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The general instruction for the orders for opening fire were, in that situation, as from 16th April onwards, is that if you came under direct fire, in other words the fire was definitely directed at you as an individual, then you were well within your rights to return fire.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: So on the day when fire was directed at you, you thought that you were not aimed at physically because you did not return fire, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was aimed at directly by approximately six individuals, and the number of reasons that prevented me from opening fire were one, by the time I would have traversed my turret round to face the rear, because at that time we were forward-facing, the individuals would have already taken cover, which I observed through my rear observation scope. Also, it would have been dangerous of me to return fire because I would have been returning fire in the direction of the garage echelon, and also in that area was the bulk fuel installation unit and other obviously UN forces, so they could have been caught in any fire, and so therefore, they are the main two reasons that I did not return fire.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Speaking of the burial which you took part in, were there repeated missions? Did you have to do this several times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was the only mission that I did on that particular day. I did no further missions in retrieving of dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you take an active part in the choice of -- in choosing the place where the bodies would be buried according to the Muslim ritual, or were you tasked to go with diggers and help people be buried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area that the -- what was selected for the graves, I am under the impression that that was already preselected before we collected the bodies, due to the fact that when we returned from the first collection from the school, we moved on to the field and by that stage the combat tractor or digger had arrived and started digging, so that was already preselected. All we did, or I did, was to escort the vehicle back and forth on two occasions to pick up the bodies from the school and take them to the field itself.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: You never escorted General Blaskic, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR KEHOE
utterances.text: Had you heard of the HOS, of the Vitezovi, of the Jokeri, since you spent a lot of time there, since you only mentioned HVO? Were you aware of the presence of other paramilitary forces, more or less directly depending or under the HVO command, or did you only hear of the HVO as an organised force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we had also heard of what we call the HOS force, which we were informed was sort of their elite soldiers. On one particular occasion, I did happen to see three to four busloads of HOS in black uniforms with balaclavas moving from the Vitez area along towards the Novi Travnik checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Sergeant Major, it was a long testimony, the Tribunal is very thankful for your coming to testify, as summoned by the Prosecutor. You can now return to further missions with our thanks. Usher, can you make sure that Sergeant Major Hughes can be led out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Prosecutor, you do not have any other witnesses, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr President, your Honours, we do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, I think that in the future we will have to make sure that we do not have those interruptions that are very harmful for our proceedings, you know it is difficult to schedule anything firmly. It is a bit of a problem, is it not? I suppose you agree with the judges in saying so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr President. We have had some problems with some witnesses and some difficulties making mid course corrections and bringing people from Bosnia. We apologise and, of course, we will make every effort to ensure that it does not happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Kehoe. So we are going to adjourn. There will be no hearing tomorrow. On Friday morning, I remind you that at 9.30, we have scheduled a motion hearing, both the Defence and the Prosecution wanted to argue, for not too much of a time, I hope, I hope you shall be brief, to develop your written arguments on hearsay to start with, on hearsay evidence and also as to the Defence's motion to review a decision issued by the Trial Chamber as to exculpatory testimony and material. So we are going to hear arguments on the two motions, and then we will have a short break and will return in closed session and we will have a status conference to deal with two topics which are very dear to my heart. On the one hand, we will have the repercussions of the recent judgment issued by the Appeals Chamber on subpoena; many subpoenas have been issued or requested since February. We all agreed to suspend, to stay their use and to wait until the Appeals Chamber had issued a decision to see what we would do with the subpoenas as issued either by Judge McDonald's Chamber or by a single judge, as was the case once with Judge Jan. Then we will talk about the problems involved in the proceedings and the duration thereof and what we can do to make sure that we can keep the trial within a reasonable time period as is put by all international treaties. The hearing is adjourned and we will resume again at 9.30 on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: on Friday, 28th November 1997)
